bill.title: American Music Tourism Act of 2025

industries.rationale: The bill explicitly directs federal promotion of tourism to music festivals, concert venues, and music-related attractions, which would increase visitor traffic and revenue for the music and entertainment sector.
Federal promotion of domestic and international tourism to music and sports attractions would directly increase demand for hotels, travel services, and related hospitality businesses.

bill.plainSummary: This bill directs the National Travel and Tourism Office within the Department of Commerce to actively promote tourism to music festivals, concert venues, and other music-related sites in the United States, targeting both domestic and international travelers. It also expands the office's existing sports-promotion duties to include international tourism for sports events. The office must report its activities and results to Congress within one year and every two years thereafter.

bill.title: TAKE IT DOWN Act

industries.rationale: The bill directly imposes new content moderation obligations and 48-hour removal requirements on social media platforms and user-generated content websites.
New criminal prohibitions and mandatory restitution provisions would generate litigation and enforcement work related to intimate image publication.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would make it a federal crime to publish intimate images or videos of someone online without their consent, including computer-generated deepfakes, when the publication is intended to cause harm or involves a minor. Social media platforms and similar websites would be required to remove such content within 48 hours after receiving a complaint from the person depicted. Violators would face criminal penalties including prison time, fines, and mandatory restitution to victims.

bill.title: Patients Deserve Price Tags Act
bill.latestActionText: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 522.
subjects: Department of Health and Human Services
Drug safety, medical device, and laboratory regulation

industries.rationale: The bill directly imposes new price-disclosure obligations on hospitals and surgical centers, changing their administrative and compliance requirements.
Medical device costs must be included in the price estimates, affecting how device manufacturers' products are priced and disclosed to patients.
Price transparency requirements may affect how insurers negotiate rates and how patients understand their coverage and out-of-pocket costs.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would require hospitals, ambulatory surgical centers, and other healthcare facilities to provide patients with upfront price estimates for scheduled procedures and services. The estimates would need to include costs for the facility, physicians, anesthesia, medical devices, and other associated charges. Facilities that fail to provide these price disclosures could face civil penalties.

bill.title: Rural Broadband Protection Act of 2025

industries.rationale: The bill directly regulates eligibility and vetting for broadband providers seeking federal subsidies to deploy networks in rural areas.
Some internet service providers and broadband infrastructure companies in the technology sector may apply for these rural deployment funds.

bill.plainSummary: This bill directs the Federal Communications Commission to create a formal screening process for companies applying for federal funding to build broadband networks in rural and other high-cost areas. Applicants would need to prove they have the technical skills, financial resources, and realistic business plans to complete the projects, and the FCC would check their track record with other government broadband programs. Companies that fail to meet these standards after applying would face financial penalties, and only those who pass the vetting would receive funding.

bill.title: A joint resolution proposing an amendment to the Constitution of the United States relating to contributions and expenditures intended to affect elections.
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

industries.rationale: Organizations that spend money to influence elections would face new potential restrictions on their expenditures and fundraising.
The amendment would create new constitutional authority to regulate campaign finance, directly affecting election law practice and lobbying activity.
Limits on campaign spending could affect demand for political advertising across broadcast, digital, and print media platforms.
The amendment's authorization to distinguish between natural persons and corporations could affect how financial institutions participate in election-related spending.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution proposes a constitutional amendment that would allow Congress and state governments to set limits on how much money candidates and others can raise and spend to influence elections. It would also permit lawmakers to treat corporations and other legal entities differently from individual people, including by prohibiting those entities from spending money on elections. The amendment would require ratification by three-fourths of the states to take effect.

bill.title: Ending Improper Payments to Deceased People Act

industries.rationale: Life insurers and annuity providers rely on death records to process claims and prevent fraudulent payments to deceased beneficiaries.
Banks and financial institutions use death records to manage accounts, prevent fraud, and comply with payment verification requirements.

bill.plainSummary: This bill makes permanent the Treasury Department's access to Social Security death records to prevent payments from being sent to deceased individuals. It requires the Social Security Administration to have clear and convincing evidence before marking someone as deceased in its master file. If someone is incorrectly listed as dead, the SSA can notify federal and state agencies that provide benefits so the error can be corrected.

bill.title: A joint resolution to direct the removal of United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Venezuela that have not been authorized by Congress.
bill.latestActionText: Point of order that the measure is not entitled to expedited procedures under 50 U.S.C. 1546(a) raised against the measure agreed to in Senate by Yea-Nay Vote. 50 - 50. Record Vote Number: 9.

industries.rationale: The resolution would directly affect the deployment and operational scope of U.S. Armed Forces and defense contractors supporting military operations in the Venezuela region.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would require the President to end any U.S. military operations in or against Venezuela unless Congress has formally declared war or authorized the use of force. It preserves the President's authority to defend the United States from an armed attack or imminent threat. The measure addresses congressional oversight of military deployments and the constitutional division of war powers.

bill.title: A resolution supporting the goals and ideals of National Safe Digging Month.
bill.latestActionText: Submitted in the Senate, considered, and agreed to without amendment and with a preamble by Unanimous Consent. (consideration: CR S1789-1790; text: CR S1788)

industries.rationale: Electric and gas utilities own underground infrastructure that the resolution aims to protect through safe digging practices.
Telecom providers operate underground cable networks that could be damaged by excavation without proper location calls.
Construction firms and excavators are directly encouraged to use 811 services before digging projects.
Water and wastewater utilities maintain underground pipes that safe digging practices are designed to protect.

bill.plainSummary: This resolution expresses support for National Safe Digging Month and encourages homeowners and excavators to contact 811 before digging to locate underground utility lines. It is a non-binding resolution that does not change any laws or create new requirements. The measure promotes awareness of existing call-before-you-dig practices.

bill.title: Stop Russian Market Manipulation Act
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

industries.rationale: The bill directly restricts imports of eight specific metals and minerals, affecting companies that source, process, or trade these materials.
Manufacturers that rely on platinum-group metals, nickel, copper, or zinc as inputs would face supply-chain changes and potentially higher costs.
Defense contractors use platinum-group metals and specialty alloys in aerospace and weapons systems, making supply sourcing relevant.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would ban the import of eight minerals—platinum, palladium, rhodium, ruthenium, nickel, copper, zinc, and braggite—if they are produced in Russia or by Russian entities. The ban would also cover minerals obtained through swaps or other arrangements designed to evade the restriction. The prohibition would remain in effect until one year after the President certifies that Russia has ended hostilities against Ukraine, and would resume if Russia restarts hostilities within three years.
